source: Zilberstein (1996) Using anytime algorithms in intelligent systems
finding: Defines anytime algorithms: quality improves as time grows. Lists seven properties: measurable quality, recognizable quality, monotonicity, consistency, diminishing returns, interruptibility, preemptability.
numbers: Seven properties. Example domains: signal interpretation, real-time diagnosis, robot control.
quote: Fifth is diminishing returns: The improvement in solution quality is larger at the early stages of the computation
limits: Review article, no LLM data. Properties are design ideals, not always met.
agent_relevance: Our agent should treat each attempt as having a performance profile; G6 (never abstain) needs a best-so-far answer at every point.

source: Zilberstein (1996) Using anytime algorithms in intelligent systems (interruptible vs contract)
finding: Interruptible algorithms give an answer at any stop time. Contract algorithms need the time budget known in advance. A standard transformation (Russell and Zilberstein 1991) turns a contract algorithm into an interruptible one with a small constant penalty.
numbers: Constant penalty; this article says 'small, constant penalty' and gives no exact factor.
limits: Exact factor comes from the cited 1991 paper, not read here.
agent_relevance: LLM thinking with a fixed token budget is a contract algorithm; a loop that restarts with doubling budgets makes it interruptible at bounded cost. Supports G12.

source: Zilberstein (1996) Using anytime algorithms in intelligent systems (monotonicity by best-so-far)
finding: If quality is recognizable at run time, monotonicity can be guaranteed by returning the best result so far instead of the latest.
limits: Needs a reliable quality check. For LLM answers there is often none.
agent_relevance: Matches G6: keep the best attempt so far. It also shows why G3 (a real check) matters: without recognizable quality, best-so-far cannot be chosen.

source: Dean and Boddy (1988) An analysis of time-dependent planning (as cited in Zilberstein 1996)
finding: Coined anytime algorithms and deliberation scheduling with performance profiles (time-dependent planning).
limits: Not opened; known only through Zilberstein's description.
agent_relevance: Origin of the time-versus-quality framing used for test-time compute.

source: Simon (1955) A behavioral model of rational choice (named in task key works)
finding: Founding claim: real agents search until an aspiration level is met, not for the optimum. Not opened this session.
limits: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Basis for a stop rule: stop when a check passes, not when compute runs out. Links to G6.

source: Qi et al. (2025) Optimizing Anytime Reasoning via Budget Relative Policy Optimization (AnytimeReasoner)
finding: Trains a reasoning model so that its thinking can be cut at any point and summarised. Samples the thinking budget from a prior and rewards the summary answer at each budget. Beats GRPO at all thinking budgets.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, 40,315 math problems (DeepScaleR), 1 epoch. Budgets 2000/4000/6000/8000 tokens, 8 rollouts per question, 4 answers per budget. Eval on AIME24, AMC22, MATH500, Minerva, OlympiadBench at 32 budgets from 0 to 8000. 320 samples per question for AMC and AIME, 80 for others. Under 10% training overhead vs GRPO. 7B model: up to about 5 absolute points better anytime accuracy.
quote: the system can be interrupted at any point during computation, providing the best possible solution so far
limits: Small and mid models, math only. Final-accuracy gain at 7B was noisy.
agent_relevance: Direct modern version of Zilberstein's interruptible algorithm. Shows anytime quality can be trained, and that the summary step is key (decoupled summary policy).

source: Qi et al. (2025) AnytimeReasoner ablations
finding: Three parts help separately: dense per-budget rewards, a separately trained summary policy under uniform budgets, and a variance-reduction baseline using earlier budgets. Even the variant trained only for the max budget beat GRPO at all budgets.
numbers: Anytime accuracy = mean over budgets {2000,4000,6000,8000}; final accuracy = at 8000. Small budgets favour the uniform prior; large budgets converge across priors.
quote: Empirically, we observe that generating a high-quality summary is critical for both final and anytime performance.
limits: Ablations on 1.5B only.
agent_relevance: A forced-answer step at a cut point matters as much as the thinking itself. A scaffold should have a dedicated 'answer from partial work' slot.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1: Controlling How Long A Reasoning Model Thinks
finding: Length-controlled policy optimisation (LCPO) trains a 1.5B model to follow a stated token target. It beats S1 budget forcing at short budgets.
numbers: L1 vs S1: 100-150% relative and 20-25% absolute gain at 512 and 1024 token budgets. Log-linear scaling slope 0.24 for L1 vs 0.37 for S1. L1-Exact about 1% below DeepScaleR-4K. Short reasoning models beat their originals by up to 10% at equal length; a 1.5B model matched GPT-4o at equal token budget.
limits: Trained for contract-style budgets (budget known in advance), not interruption. 1.5B model.
agent_relevance: Contract-type control works when the budget is declared up front. A scaffold that knows its budget should state it in the prompt.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: cut thinking by inserting the end token, or lengthen it by appending 'Wait'. s1-32B trained on 1,000 examples. Accuracy rises with thinking and extrapolates a little.
numbers: AIME24 from 50% to 57% by forcing 'Wait' 2/4/6 times beyond the trained range. Budget forcing ablation (Table 3): control 100%, slope 15, AIME24 performance 56.7. Token-conditional control alone: control 40%, slope -24.
limits: Gains flatten or reverse at long lengths; context-window limited. Single model family, 30 AIME24 questions.
agent_relevance: Shows the performance profile is rising then flat: the shape Simon and Zilberstein predict. Also shows forced cut-off is a workable interrupt.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: rejection sampling on AIME24
finding: Sampling until the answer is short enough gave an inverse scaling: shorter-thinking samples were more accurate than longer ones.
numbers: Needed an average of 655, 97, 8, 3, 2 and 1 tries per sample for caps of 3500, 4000, 5000, 8000 and 16000 thinking tokens. Authors show a question solved at a 4000 cap but not at 8000, where the model backtracked a lot.
limits: Authors flag this as a hypothesis; one example inspected.
agent_relevance: Quality is not monotone in time for a given sample. Long traces can hurt, so best-so-far with a check beats last-answer.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Best use of a fixed compute budget depends on question difficulty. Adaptive allocation beats a fixed strategy and can beat best-of-N with up to 4x less compute.
numbers: Beam search beats best-of-N at small budgets and on hard questions; best-of-N wins at large budgets and on easy questions. Compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N using up to 4x less test-time compute (e.g. 16 vs 64 generations; 64 vs 256 for revisions). Difficulty in five bins; model-predicted difficulty costs extra inference, and gains shrink at high budgets versus oracle bins.
limits: MATH benchmark, PaLM 2-S*. Oracle bins use ground truth; predicted difficulty gives smaller gains.
agent_relevance: This is metareasoning (value of computation) applied to LLMs. An orchestrator in code can pick depth versus breadth by estimated difficulty (G12).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) rises log-linearly with number of samples over four orders of magnitude. Selection methods (majority vote, reward models) plateau beyond several hundred samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250 samples, above single-sample SOTA of 43%.
limits: Gain only converts to accuracy where an automatic verifier exists.
agent_relevance: Quality-versus-samples profile has diminishing returns; a verifier is what makes it anytime-usable (G3).

source: Han et al. (2024) Token-Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning (TALE)
finding: Putting a token budget in the prompt shrinks chain of thought. Budget choice matters: too small a budget is ignored (token elasticity). TALE estimates a budget per problem.
numbers: Example: output fell from 258 to 86 tokens with a 50-token budget, but a 10-token budget gave 157 tokens. TALE-EP: 81.03% accuracy vs 83.75% for vanilla CoT, using 32% of the tokens and 41% of the expense.
quote: when the token budget is relatively small, LLMs often fail to follow the given token budget
limits: Prompt-only budget control is unreliable below a model-specific floor. Small benchmark set.
agent_relevance: Declare a budget, but never rely on the model to obey it; the program must enforce the cut (section 1 of the schema).

source: Xu et al. (2025) Scalable Chain of Thoughts via Elastic Reasoning (E1)
finding: Separate the thinking budget from the solution budget. Always protect the solution segment. Budget-constrained rollout in GRPO teaches the model to answer from truncated thinking.
numbers: E1-Math-1.5B on AIME2024: 35.0% vs 27.1% L1-Max, 24.2% L1-Exact, 41.0% original unconstrained model. Also tested on MATH500, LiveCodeBench, Codeforces; generalises to unseen budgets.
limits: Loses about 6 points against the unconstrained model on AIME2024.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as AnytimeReasoner: reserve tokens for a final answer so a cut never leaves nothing. Supports G6.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling
finding: More thinking (forced 'Wait') first raises accuracy, then lowers it. Authors explain this as added output variance, not better reasoning.
numbers: One panel: accuracy 82.2% to 87.3% as mean thinking tokens go 385 to 1100, then falls to 70.3% at 15,980 tokens. Parallel thinking (majority vote) at the same budget: up to 20% higher accuracy; at 16K tokens about 22% above Wait and 47% above Exact-thinking budget control.
limits: Performance profile is non-monotone, a failed assumption of Zilberstein property 3 for raw LLM thinking. Open reasoning models, math benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Do not trust last-answer-at-longest-time. Use code-side selection across attempts (G5) and stop on signal (G1).

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: At thought-switch points, prompt the model for a trial answer and exit if its confidence is high. Training-free.
numbers: 10 benchmarks, 11 reasoning models: chain length cut by 19.1% to 80.1% on average while accuracy changes by +0.3% to +5.0%.
limits: Model confidence is the stop signal, which can be overconfident; varies by model.
agent_relevance: A stop rule based on answer confidence at natural breakpoints. Compatible with our rule that stopping needs a signal, but confidence alone is a weak signal (G3).

source: Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning (2025)
finding: Models usually reach their final answer after about 60% of the reasoning steps. Three stop methods: answer consistency, boosting end-of-reasoning probability, learned probe on activations.
numbers: Convergence after 60% of steps on math. Five benchmarks, five open models. Answer Consistency cut tokens by over 40% on NaturalQuestions with higher accuracy.
quote: models typically converge to their final answers after 60% of the reasoning steps
limits: Open-weight models; savings differ by task.
agent_relevance: Repeated identical trial answers are a cheap, code-checkable stop signal. Same-model agreement is still not independent proof (G4).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: probing hidden states
finding: A probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct, even before the answer is written. Used as an exit rule.
numbers: Probes: ROC-AUC above 0.7 and expected calibration error below 0.1 in-distribution. Using the probe to exit cut inference tokens by 24% with no performance loss.
limits: Needs hidden-state access and per-dataset training; out-of-distribution transfer weaker.
agent_relevance: Shows quality is partly recognizable inside the model, but needs open weights. Not available to a prompt-only scaffold.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Sample in small windows and stop when a window is unanimous. Cuts samples with similar accuracy.
numbers: Average samples cut: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%.
limits: Agreement among samples from one model is not truth (our G4). Savings are largest on easy tasks.
agent_relevance: A concrete anytime rule in code: stop sampling at first unanimous window. Cheap and program-controlled.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking (NoThinking)
finding: Skipping the thinking block and sampling many short answers beats thinking at low token budgets.
numbers: ACM 23 at 700 tokens: 51.3 NoThinking vs 28.9 Thinking. With parallel best-of-N, matches Thinking that takes up to 9x longer latency.
limits: Advantage shrinks as budgets grow; depends on a verifier or confidence selector.
agent_relevance: At small budgets the quality-time curve favours many cheap attempts over one long one. Supports parallel attempts with a code selector.

source: Manvi, Singh, Ermon (2024) Adaptive Inference-Time Compute
finding: The model emits one token predicting whether restarting would give a better answer. Used to stop sampling or prune weak samples early.
numbers: Llama 3.1 8B AlpacaEval win rate vs GPT-4 from 21% to 34% with 16 samples; GSM8K from 84% to 91% (abstract and first page read only).
limits: Needs fine-tuning on preference data; only the first page was read.
agent_relevance: A learned value-of-computation signal. A prompt-only version would be a judged step, which our schema distrusts.

source: Cross-paper comparison of anytime-safe LLM thinking (Qi 2025, Aggarwal 2025, Xu 2025, Yang 2025, Li 2024)
finding: Three ways to make LLM thinking anytime-safe: train for random cut points (AnytimeReasoner), train to follow a stated budget (L1, E1), or add an external stop rule (DEER, ESC, convergence). They trade training cost against portability.
numbers: Training-based: 1.5B models, 8-GPU runs of about 30 hours (AnytimeReasoner). Training-free: DEER saves 19-80% tokens; ESC saves 34-84% samples.
limits: Comparison is ours, across different models and benchmarks, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: For a no-training scaffold, only the external-rule family applies. Cut points plus a forced-answer slot are free to add.

source: Snell et al. (2024) sequential vs parallel and difficulty
finding: Easy questions do best with sequential revision; hard questions do best with parallel search. At a fixed budget there is an ideal mix.
numbers: Compute-optimal oracle and predicted difficulty both beat the parallel baseline; gains from predicted bins are smaller at higher budgets.
limits: MATH only, one model family.
agent_relevance: Supports a router that sets depth by cheap difficulty probes, costed against the budget (G7).

source: Hansen and Zilberstein (2001) Monitoring and control of anytime algorithms
finding: Dynamic-programming monitoring policies decide when to stop an anytime algorithm using a performance profile and time cost. Recalled, not opened.
limits: Not opened; recalled, not verified this session.
agent_relevance: Formal basis for a program-side stop rule: stop when expected gain falls below time cost.

source: Horvitz (1987/1990) flexible computation (as cited in Zilberstein 1996)
finding: Parallel line to Dean and Boddy: value of computation under time-critical decisions. Mentioned in Zilberstein's article; original not opened.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Ties to value-of-computation signals that LLM work now approximates with probes.
